blocks.html: This word Arrest, in our French tongue, is taken in two ways. The first, for a final judgment and decree of a sovereign court; and so many think that it is drawn from the Greek ἄρεστον, which is as much as to say an ordinance of a magistrate. Whence it seems also, says that great Budé, that we err in writing and pronouncing it with a double R, seeing that ἄρεστον, from which it is drawn, is written only with a single R a. The second, for a kind of imprisonment, proceeding from the command and injunction of the magistrate made to some person not to stir from a certain place which he assigns to him b: as in our context.

notes.citation: Guillaume Budé (Guil. Budée), Annotationes in Pandectas, on the last law of Digest 1.9 (De senatoribus; l. fin. = D. 1.9.12, Ulpian), at its end
notes.original: Guil. Budée en la Loy fin. ſur la fin. D. de ſenator.
notes.gloss: Budé's Annotationes (1508) are arranged as a commentary on the Digest; the passage deriving arrest from ἀρεστόν stands under this law. Locus not verified against the printed Annotationes.

notes.citation: Digest 43.29 (De homine libero exhibendo), l. 2 (D. 43.29.2, Venuleius; the title has four laws, and the second is taken as printed); Digest 35.1 (De condicionibus et demonstrationibus et causis et modis eorum quae in testamento scribuntur), the law containing the paragraph beginning Titio centum (the law's incipit is not printed; fragment not identified)
notes.original: l. ij. D. de lib. exhib. l. P. Tirio centũ. D. de con. & demon.
notes.gloss: The print's P. is its sort for the paragraph sign §, and Tirio a wrong sort for Titio. Cited for the Roman sense of being kept or detained in a place without being in a prison: the interdict for producing a free man wrongfully held, and a legacy conditioned on the legatee's not leaving a place.
